source: Castagna, Sassoon, Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought: steering LLM reasoning with argumentative querying
finding: A Toulmin-based pipeline makes the model draft a reasoning plan, answer 8 critical questions about it, and proceed only if enough are answered yes. Judged on MT-Bench reasoning and math questions, it beat both the plain baseline and chain of thought for most models. This is the closest test of Gap 1: critical questions as a verify step, scored on answer quality.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5-pro-001, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.1-70B-Instruct, Nemotron-51B). Judge GPT-4o, 1-10 score, re-asked until the same score came up 3 times. Mean gain of CQoT: +4.61% (reasoning) and +5.4% (math) over the baseline and CoT means. CQoT best in 18 of 20 comparisons (2 domains x 5 models x vs baseline and vs CoT), joint best in 1. Nemotron-51B scored higher with CoT than CQoT on reasoning. Pipeline loops up to 11 iterations. Paper text: a conclusion is ruled out unless a majority of the 8 CQs are answered yes (a secondary summary said 7 of 8).
quote: a conclusion being ruled out unless a majority of the CQs are answered positively
limits: Judge is GPT-4o scoring against a reference; MT-Bench reasoning and math sets are small (sample size not stated in text read); no accuracy against ground truth; tokens NOT matched (CQoT is a multi-step loop, CoT is one pass), so it does not isolate the checklist from extra compute. Ablation without steps 2-3 (no CQs) still beat baseline, with the full pipeline higher. Questions follow Toulmin parts, not ARS. Authors suspect a ~70B size threshold for instruction following.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a structured critical-question gate can help reasoning answers on frontier models, but not proof that ARS beats a generic check at equal tokens. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Calvo Figueras and Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation (v3 HTML)
finding: LLMs asked to write Walton-style critical questions for an argument produce mostly weak ones. No zero-shot model gets above 57% useful. Asking an LLM to label question usefulness directly agrees poorly with humans.
numbers: 220 interventions, 4,976 annotated questions; validation 186 interventions with 4,136 questions (67.46% useful); test 34 interventions with 806 questions (42.68% useful). 11 models zero-shot; top average score Claude 3.5 Sonnet 56.32, GPT-4o 54.47, o4-mini 54.14, lowest Qwen2.5-7B 43.40. Annotator kappa rose from 0.19-0.26 to 0.54. Direct LLM labelling without references: agreement below 0.1. Reference-based Claude judge: 0.57 match with humans.
limits: Task is generating questions about short interventions, not using them to improve an answer. Scores are averages over three reference-based metrics, not a plain percent useful per model. Zero-shot only, no prompt tuning. Numbers come from a fetch summary of the HTML page.
agent_relevance: If the agent writes its own critical questions, expect generic ones; a fixed ARS question list may be safer than free generation.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Generic 'review your answer' prompts without outside feedback do not raise reasoning accuracy and often lower it. Gains reported elsewhere came from oracle labels, from unfair comparison to self-consistency, or from weak initial prompts. This is the generic-check baseline that Gap 1 compares against.
numbers: Intrinsic self-correction, 1/3/5 calls: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0 (row order read from extracted table text). With oracle labels the same methods gain a lot. Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at equal numbers of responses.
limits: Short verifiable answers (math, multiple choice, multi-hop QA), not open-ended essays. Models are GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2, not 2026 frontier models. A criteria-specific critique was not the focus.
agent_relevance: Default stance: a generic Verify pass is not free accuracy. An ARS pass must be tested against it and against self-consistency at equal calls.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning (ICLR)
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 CoT papers plus 20 datasets x 14 models. CoT helps mostly on math, symbolic and logical tasks; elsewhere gains are close to zero. On MMLU almost all of the gain sits on questions containing an equals sign.
numbers: Mean CoT gain: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9 points. Top three categories 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. Other categories 56.8 vs 56.1. Authors state up to 95% of CoT gain on MMLU is on questions with an equals sign.
quote: directly generating the answer without CoT leads to almost identical accuracy as CoT unless the question or model's response contains an equals sign
limits: Measures CoT on answering, not CoT before an argument-quality verdict. Argument judging is a rating task, likely in the non-symbolic bucket, but it was not tested.
agent_relevance: Weak indirect support for Gap 6: expect little gain, possible loss, from reasoning-before-verdict on non-symbolic judging. Needs a direct test.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse (v4)
finding: On tasks where deliberation hurts people, CoT also hurt frontier models. Evidence that explicit reasoning is not always safe for judgment-like tasks, including for reasoning models.
numbers: Six tasks; three show significant drops, three are mixed. Artificial grammar learning, direct vs CoT accuracy: GPT-4o 87.5 vs 64.4 (-23.1), Claude 3 Opus 70.7 vs 62.7 (-8.0), Gemini 1.5 Pro 68.0 vs 61.95 (-6.05), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 vs 67.7 (+1.8, not significant). On a subset, o1-preview is 36.3 points lower than GPT-4o. Exceptions task: GPT-4o needed 2.9 vs 12.5 (CoT) steps to learn labels, +331%.
limits: Tasks are psychology paradigms (grammar learning, face recognition, exceptions), not argument evaluation. Table layout read from extracted text; use headline figures.
agent_relevance: Supports Gap 6 as a live risk: CoT before a verdict can cut accuracy on judgment tasks even for frontier models. Test verdict-first vs reasoning-first in the ARS judge.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: LLM judges prefer text they wrote, and the strength of self-preference rises with how well the model recognises its own text. Fine-tuning for self-recognition raises self-preference linearly.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2 on XSUM and CNN/DailyMail summaries. GPT-4 identifies its own text 73.5% of the time against two other LLMs and humans; all three models above 50%. GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 above 90% self-recognition after fine-tuning on 500 examples. Position bias: pairwise preference reverses when order is swapped in 25% (GPT-4), 58% (GPT-3.5), 89% (Llama) of cases.
limits: Summarisation quality, not argument quality. Self-preference may partly reflect real quality; authors control with fine-tuning on unrelated tasks. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: when the agent judges its own answer in S8, expect inflated scores. Use a different model or a blind rewrite for the judge, and swap option order.

source: Ye et al. (2025) Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge (CALM, ICLR)
finding: Twelve judge biases were measured automatically. Judges are often swayed by sentiment, authority cues, bandwagon and own-model answers. Fallacy oversight was also measured: the strongest models mostly caught flawed reasoning.
numbers: Robustness rate (1.0 = no bias), six judges. Fact-related set: verbosity .884-.977 (GPT-4o .977, Claude-3.5 .952), fallacy-oversight .917-.985 (GPT-4o .984, Claude-3.5 .985, ChatGPT .917), sentiment .651-.804. Alignment set: position .566-.832; bandwagon .610 (Claude-3.5) to .791 (GPT-4o); authority .662-.865. Most models rate their own outputs higher even when anonymised.
limits: Math/fact and alignment datasets, not argument corpora; biases injected by GPT-4o rewrite; 2024 models. Hedging was not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: fluent or confident-sounding text and authority cues are real judge levers. Use paired controls (rewrite with and without hedges) before treating hedge = low grounds as a defect.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (ICML)
finding: A single irrelevant sentence added to a maths problem sharply cut accuracy. Self-consistency and an instruction to ignore irrelevant information recover part of the loss. This is the relevance-failure case for context the agent reads.
numbers: GSM-IC built from GSM8K; Codex and GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003). Fewer than 30% of base problems solved consistently across all distractor variants. Self-consistency with 20 samples: micro accuracy up by more than 11 points; 0-CoT gain 35.5 points; best macro accuracy after all fixes only 45%. Correct answer is among the 20 samples for 99.7% of problems. The instruction to ignore irrelevant information consistently helps CoT, LTM and PROGRAM.
limits: Arithmetic with a planted irrelevant sentence, 2022-era models. Irrelevance is topical, not fallacious support.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 10: a relevance instruction helps a little; sampling gives the larger gain. Relevance is the cheap part of ARS to add.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2024) Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models (Findings ACL)
finding: A verify step built as separate targeted questions, answered without seeing the draft, beats a joint check and beats CoT. Targeted probing (like a sufficiency probe) helps more than one holistic pass.
numbers: Llama 65B. Wikidata list precision 0.17 -> 0.36 (hallucinated entities 2.95 -> 0.68). MultiSpanQA F1 0.39 -> 0.48 (+23%). Longform FACTSCORE: few-shot 55.9; CoVe joint 60.8; factored 63.7; factor+revise 71.4. Llama 2 70B Chat zero-shot 41.3 vs CoT 41.1. Facts kept fell 16.6 -> 12.3.
limits: Factual hallucination, not argument quality. Compute is higher than baseline; no equal-token comparison. Llama 65B, 2023.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: supports running a sufficiency probe as a separate pass with the draft hidden, not a full triad in one pass. Gap 5: closed-book verification of factual claims can work.

source: Cook, Rocktaschel, Foerster, Aumiller, Wang (2024) TICKing All the Boxes: Generated Checklists Improve LLM Evaluation and Generation
finding: A task-specific YES/NO checklist used as the self-critique (STICK) improved answers, while a free-form self-critique (Self-Refine) made them worse. Closest direct test of checklist vs generic check on end-task quality (Gap 1), though for instruction following, not ARS.
numbers: LiveBench, one refinement step: STICK reasoning +7.8 absolute (Command-R+, abstract); overall Command-R+ +3.8 and GPT-4o +0.8, while vanilla Self-Refine lowered scores (for example GPT-4o language -25.2, instructions -14.0). Command-R+ InFoBench +6.5 and WildBench +7.1 over rounds, above Self-Refine. Best-of-N: +5.1 InFoBench and +5.3 WildBench over greedy; beat direct self-scoring.
limits: Instruction-following checklists, not argument criteria. Command-R+ and GPT-4o, 2024 only; GPT-4o gain small (0.8). Gains fade after one iteration on LiveBench. Token cost of checklist not matched against Self-Refine. Table layout from extracted text.
agent_relevance: Best present evidence that a structured checklist beats an open check-your-answer prompt. Predicts an ARS checklist helps most when concrete and answer-specific. Gap 1 informed, not closed.

source: Cook et al. (2024) TICK: judge and human agreement with checklists
finding: Using LLM-made checklists in the judge raised exact agreement with human preferences. Giving human raters a checklist raised their agreement too.
numbers: Exact agreement between LLM judge and human preferences 46.4% -> 52.2% vs direct scoring. Inter-annotator agreement on WildBench scores 0.194 -> 0.256 with checklists.
limits: Absolute agreement stays modest; WildBench and instruction following, not arguments.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a checklist raises rater agreement but does not fix low-agreement items; use it to calibrate the sufficiency judge, and expect modest levels.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Verbalised confidence from models is high and badly calibrated. Sampling several answers and agreement among them help somewhat, and no method wins everywhere.
numbers: 5 LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat, five dataset types. Verbalised confidence mostly 80-100%. Black-box vs white-box failure prediction AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605. Calibration improves with Top-K and consistency prompts; failure prediction stays weak on hard tasks.
limits: 2023 models; short-answer tasks; says nothing about argument-based confidence. No Bayesian argument-strength arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: do not turn a checklist verdict into a self-stated percent. If a confidence is reported, derive it from sample agreement. Hahn-Oaksford probability ratings remain untested for LLMs.

source: Manakul, Liusie, Gales (2023) SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection (EMNLP)
finding: A model can flag its own unsupported factual claims without retrieval by comparing a sentence against several resampled answers. Prompt-based consistency checking worked best.
numbers: WikiBio passages from GPT-3 (N=20 samples). Sentence-level AUC-PR for non-factual detection: random 72.96, GPT-3 token probabilities 80.7-87.5, SelfCheckGPT BERTScore 81.96, QA 84.26, unigram 85.63, NLI 92.50, Prompt 93.42. Factual-sentence AUC-PR with Prompt 67.09. Passage-level Pearson 78.32.
limits: Biography text where hallucinations are common; GPT-3 era; 20 samples is costly. Checks consistency, not truth: a consistently wrong model passes.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: closed-book checks of factual premises can work through resampling agreement. Consider 3-5 samples, and flag low agreement as weak support.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies, section 3.3 (first 100k characters via fetch)
finding: SEP states Johnson and Blair define a fallacy as an argument that violates one of the criteria of good argument. Acceptability is relative to audiences, while relevance and sufficiency stay undefined and intuitive. Sufficiency is a matter of degree and has no numerical expression in their account.
numbers: No numbers. Mentions Johnson's 1987 frequency requirement: a mistake must be common enough to count as a fallacy.
quote: Acceptability is defined relative to audiences
limits: Secondary source via a fetch summary, not the 1977/2006 books. Govier appears only in passing.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the checklist prompt should fix the audience for acceptability, treat relevance and sufficiency as graded, and not label rare slips as fallacies.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Argument and Argumentation, sections 2.1-2.5, 4.3, 5.1
finding: The entry does not discuss ARS or conductive arguments. It says argument types have different standards (validity for deduction, cogency for induction). On a Bayesian view, some supposed fallacies can be good arguments depending on the informational context. Virtue theory is an alternative to judging arguments in abstraction from arguers.
limits: No ARS detail, so little for Gap 8; the books remain unread.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 9: one checklist cannot cover all argument types; judge by type and context. Sufficiency as degree of support matches a probabilistic confidence.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Informal Logic, section 4.1 (reread on uncertainty and conductive arguments)
finding: Truth is not always an adequate acceptability test; an acceptable premise may also need to be acceptable to this audience, and for claims without truth values it is acceptable to the degree it is reasonable. Conductive arguments support conclusions by accumulating non-decisive reasons, so sufficiency is cumulative. Hansen (2012) argues informal logic should not concern itself with premise acceptability.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Johnson and Blair (2011) for conductive arguments and Possin (2016) as a sceptic.
quote: an acceptable premise may need to be true, but also acceptable to the members of this audience
limits: Secondary summary; first 100k characters only; Govier's own conditions not listed.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: tell the checker to count reasons together for conductive cases, and ask acceptable to whom for premises that are not plain facts.

source: Search log (this run): no direct tests found of ARS or critical-question checklists vs generic checks on open answers, frontier CASA, frontier sufficiency judges on hard items, or LLM Bayesian argument strength
finding: One web search and arXiv listing attempts were made. OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv APIs returned rate-limit errors, and the shared search budget ran out. Only CQoT (d01) and TICK (d10) were found as nearby end-task tests. Absence is weak evidence: coverage was limited, so record as not found, not as nonexistent.
limits: Search limited by shared budget and API rate limits.
agent_relevance: Treat Gaps 3, 4, 6 (frontier), 9 as open; plan own experiments.
